title: United States v. Midwest Oil Co. (1915)
shortTitle: United States v. Midwest Oil Co. (1915)
summary: A long-continued executive practice known to and acquiesced in by Congress raises a presumption that the President acts with Congress's consent, so President Taft's withdrawal of public oil lands from entry was valid despite statutes opening them.
notes:
Key line: But they do clearly indicate that the long-continued practice, known to and acquiesced in by Congress, would raise a presumption that the withdrawals had been made in pursuance of its consent or of a recognized administrative power of the Executive in the management of the public lands. (Justice Lamar)

Citation: 236 U.S. 459 (1915).

sections.Parties: The appellant was the United States, which sued to recover land and the value of oil taken from it. The appellees were the Midwest Oil Company and its predecessors in interest, William T. Henshaw and associates, who had located a placer mining claim on a quarter section of public land in Wyoming after President Taft's withdrawal order. Assistant Attorney General Knaebel and the Solicitor General appeared for the Government; Joel F. Vaile and others argued for the company. The case turned on the validity of Withdrawal Order No. 5 of September 27, 1909, which took more than three million acres of oil land in California and Wyoming out of the reach of the mining laws.
sections.Material Facts: The placer mining law, Revised Statutes sections 2319 and 2329, and the Act of February 11, 1897 declared public lands containing petroleum free and open to occupation and purchase. In 1909 the Director of the Geological Survey reported that oil lands in California were being located so fast that the Government would soon own none. On September 27, 1909, President Taft issued a proclamation, Withdrawal Order No. 5, temporarily withdrawing from settlement, location and entry an area aggregating 3,041,000 acres in California and Wyoming. On January 14, 1910, Taft told Congress that his power to make such withdrawals was not clear and asked for legislation; Congress responded with the Pickett Act of June 25, 1910, authorizing future withdrawals. On March 27, 1910, six months after the order, Henshaw and others entered a quarter section of the withdrawn land in Wyoming, drilled, struck oil, and conveyed to Midwest Oil, which extracted about 50,000 barrels.
sections.Procedural History: The United States filed a bill in equity in the United States District Court for the District of Wyoming to recover the land and an accounting for the oil, arguing the location was void because the land had been withdrawn. The District Court sustained a demurrer and dismissed the bill. The Government appealed to the Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, which sent the case to the Supreme Court. The case was argued on January 9 and 12, 1914, restored to the docket for reargument on April 20, and reargued on May 7, 1914. On February 23, 1915, the Court reversed by a vote of five to three, with Justice McReynolds not participating. Justice Lamar wrote the opinion.
sections.Issue: Did the President have power, without any statute authorizing it, to withdraw public oil lands from the operation of the placer mining laws under which Congress had declared them free and open to location and purchase? The company argued that the statutes opened the land, that only Congress could close it, and that the President's order was an attempt to suspend an act of Congress. The Government argued that Presidents had made hundreds of such withdrawals for more than a century with the knowledge of Congress, that Congress had never repudiated the practice, and that this history established the power or at least implied congressional consent.
sections.Holding: The withdrawal was valid, and the bill should not have been dismissed. Before a citizen initiates a right by location, he has no vested interest in the public land statutes and no private right in land that belongs to the people. The practice of executive withdrawals of public lands from private acquisition, without specific statutory authority, dates from the early years of the Government, was constantly asserted by the Land Department, was known to Congress, and was never repudiated. Although the Executive cannot create power by his own course of action, a long-continued practice known to and acquiesced in by Congress raises a presumption that the withdrawals were made in pursuance of its consent or of a recognized administrative power in managing the public lands. The Pickett Act of 1910 did not repudiate earlier withdrawals. Reversed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Lamar declined to decide whether, as an original question, the President could withdraw lands that Congress had opened. He rested instead on practice. The record showed that Presidents had made at least 252 executive orders withdrawing land for military reservations, Indian reservations, bird reserves and other purposes without statutory authority, and that the Land Department had for decades treated the power to withdraw unappropriated lands as settled. Congress knew of these withdrawals; it received reports of them, made appropriations in reliance on them and legislated around them, yet never disaffirmed the power. Government, Lamar wrote, is a practical affair intended for practical men, and officers, lawmakers and citizens adjust to the long-continued action of the Executive on the presumption that unauthorized acts would not have been allowed to be repeated. Congress holds the public lands not only as a legislature but as a proprietor, and an owner may grant powers to his agent by implication as well as by words. The land laws are necessarily general, and the President's power to reserve land for public purposes, which the Court had recognized in earlier cases, is not different in principle from the power to withdraw it temporarily. The Court found nothing in the 1910 Pickett Act that repudiated withdrawals already made; Congress there declared that existing orders should remain in force, which was itself a recognition of the power.

topics.lrs-o-executive-orders: The case connects implied executive land-management authority to a history Congress knew and accepted, rather than emergency necessity alone.

learning.separateOpinions: Five to three. Justice Day, joined by Justices McKenna and Van Devanter, dissented. He argued that the land had been opened by statute, that the President has no power to suspend or repeal an act of Congress, that prior executive withdrawals were reservations for public uses contemplated by law and not general suspensions of the land laws, and that congressional acquiescence cannot transfer legislative power to the Executive. Justice McReynolds took no part in the decision.
